title: asking for optimal workflow
author: Legitimate_Crow804
selftext: For those of you who have successfully created a game, what specific tools, skills, tricks, or workflows do you use to speed up development, rather than constantly making small adjustments at every step along the way?

replies.author: Dignified_Cyclops
replies.body:
Not to be "that guy". Have you tried asking AI?  
Honestly the tools used depend entirely on the project.

As for speeding up development. This is where the project management hat comes on. Break work down into features and work on one feature at a time. Theres more to it, but that's a start. Do some reading on various project methodologies and work out in your head how you'd do it with AI rather than a team / few teams of people.

comments.author: AlgaeNo3373
comments.body:
A pretty big and fairly universally applicable one is in-game tuning/editing tools. Relatedly, building tools that help you build the game at an accelerated pace/more easily/less friction. 

What they look like, how they work, what they edit - all that changes dramatically by game type and genre etc. 

But basically, think of toggles, sliders, and other UI elements that let you tweak things in-game, without having to ask the AI. Most games have fonts, for example. Most people use whatever font AI gave them (and it shows). If you want to preview different fonts in-game, build/use a tool that lets you select them, change font size, swap things out, and so on previewing it live in-game, letting you tweak until perfect. 

If your game has missions or tutorials etc, you might want to build a lightweight CMS (content management system) so you can author things, re-order stuff, make text tweaks etc without diving into raw .json files or whatever. 

https://preview.redd.it/lp07860l57wh1.png?width=1185&format=png&auto=webp&s=cdd1389b1a9f30b9286f84237cc84dd36328a9b8

My current thing has hundreds of sliders to fine-tune the looks or alter volume mix of SFX, and so on. Most features added get some level of customizability.

replies.author: Count_JohnnyJ
replies.body:
in all of my projects, I had it create an editor mode for me in game that brings up a planet coaster style asset browser with the same movement and placement systems. With AI, you can customize your editors to work in a way that is already familiar to you. 

Another example: I spent years learning Maya, and could never get my head around blender. I had claude create a "maya" mode in blender that makes it look and function just like Maya to the extent it's possible without forking blender.

comments.author: Entropydemic
comments.body:
For this one-finger space adventure game, I made the Ui swappable from the left and right side of the screen.

I also mirrored multiple images of space nebula on every corner of the image and did the same for a second layer, but also had them change hue as you move, on seperate timers, so no matter where you travel to, you never appear to be in the same place. So out of several images, they never repeat. The top layer is translucent, so it looks like smoky nebula always has variety and color. They also fade when they change as you move very subtly so it doesn't feel jarring.

In other games you can put multiple layers of a skybox, which would appear like you are moving a much further distance than you are.

Little tricks like this help your mind believe you are always somewhere new.

https://preview.redd.it/1djjkj0bw7wh1.jpeg?width=717&format=pjpg&auto=webp&s=aedfd533c7a67329d2d3624dd5fdb9ccf86e1444

replies.author: Entropydemic
replies.body: I should note that if you make the colors psychedelic, when the hue changes you get a wide variety of colors changing.
